title: Serialization: JSON, Protobuf-style Binary, and Schema Evolution

questions.question: A JSON event carries "id": 9007199254740993. A Node.js consumer parses it with JSON.parse. What does it see?
options: 9007199254740993, because JSON numbers have unlimited precision
9007199254740992, because the value exceeds 2^53 and is rounded to the nearest double
A parse error, because the number has too many digits for a JSON parser
A string "9007199254740993", because large numbers are automatically quoted
questions.explanation: JSON.parse produces IEEE 754 doubles, which represent integers exactly only up to 2^53 = 9007199254740992; the next integer rounds back down to it. RFC 8259 permits any digit sequence but guarantees nothing about precision, which is why 64-bit ids are sent as strings by Twitter, Stripe, and this lesson.

questions.question: What is the varint encoding of 300?
options: ac 02
questions.explanation: 300 is binary 1_0010_1100. Split into 7-bit groups from the low end: 0101100 (0x2c) and 0000010 (0x02). The low group goes first with its continuation bit set, 0x2c | 0x80 = 0xac, then 0x02 with the bit clear. 2c 01 is the right groups without the continuation bit; 01 2c has the groups in big-endian order.

questions.question: Why does a refund of -1999 minor units cost 2 bytes as sint64 but 10 bytes as int64?
options: sint64 stores the sign in a separate byte, so only the magnitude is varint-encoded
int64 is always 8 bytes plus a 2-byte tag, while sint64 is variable-width
ZigZag maps -1999 to 3997, a small unsigned number; without it, two's complement makes -1999 a 64-bit value with all high bits set
sint64 uses base-256 digits while int64 uses base-128, so it needs fewer bytes for the same magnitude
questions.explanation: A varint spends bytes on magnitude, and a negative two's-complement number has its top bit set, so it is enormous as an unsigned value: ten varint bytes. ZigZag interleaves signs so -1999 becomes 3997, which fits in two bytes. Both types are varints; neither has a separate sign byte or a different base.

questions.question: A v1 reader meets tag byte 0x3a (field 7, wire type 2) that it does not know. What does it do?
options: Fails, because an unknown field number means the schemas are incompatible
Reads a varint length and skips that many bytes, then continues with the next tag
Skips exactly 8 bytes, the default size for an unknown field
Stops parsing and returns the fields decoded so far
questions.explanation: Wire type 2 is LENGTH_DELIMITED, so the value is a varint length followed by that many bytes; the reader can skip it without knowing what it means. That is the whole mechanism of forward compatibility. Failing or stopping would make every producer upgrade a breaking change; no wire type has a default size.

questions.question: A team changes `int64 amount_minor = 2` to `string amount_minor = 2` so that amounts can carry decimals. What happens when a new producer sends to an old consumer?
options: The old consumer parses the string as a decimal number, rounds it to minor units, and continues normally
The old consumer finds LENGTH_DELIMITED where it expects VARINT on field 2 and rejects the message as malformed
The old consumer ignores field 2 entirely and falls back to the protobuf default amount of zero minor units
Nothing breaks: changing a field's type while keeping its number is a wire-compatible change in proto3
questions.explanation: The field number is the same but the wire type changed, which violates Rule 2; the typed accessor checks the wire type and throws. A reader that did not check would misinterpret bytes instead. The correct change is a new field number for the new representation, with the old one reserved.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against hashing or signing serialized protobuf bytes directly?
options: Because protobuf bytes are compressed and the compression dictionary varies by machine
Because the encoding is not canonical: field order and default-omission can differ between encoders for the same message
Because varints are little-endian and hash functions require big-endian input
Because the tag bytes contain the field names, which differ between language bindings
questions.explanation: Two correct encoders may emit the same message with fields in different orders, or with a default value present in one and omitted in the other, producing different bytes and therefore different hashes. Signing requires a defined canonical form, as Lesson 09 used for its Merkle leaves. Tags carry numbers, not names, and varints are not compressed.
